$comment: Everyday stories, noun Concept, part 2 of 4 (concept.*, conceptAccess, domainType, enumOption). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.concept.collaboration: A support ticket often needs a quick 'I called the customer, he will pay on Friday' and a photo of the receipt. Collaboration gives every record of that kind a conversation underneath it, with mentions of colleagues and, if you want, attached files. Whoever cannot open the record cannot even tell its conversation exists.
stories.concept.composition: An invoice is a header and its lines, and no one wants to open or save half of it. Composition makes the concept the head of a small family of records that are read and written as one piece, so the document is always complete when it reaches the screen.
stories.concept.events: When a ride is completed, other parts of the app may need to know, to charge the card or ask for a rating. Events are the announcements a concept can make, like a bell in a shop. An event marked with a mode is rung automatically on every create, update or delete.
stories.concept.fields: A customer card needs a name, a phone and an address, and the form should show them in that order. Fields are the list of boxes a record has, at least one. The order in which you write them is the order people see them.
stories.concept.invariants: No two employees may share the same badge number, and a discount may never be bigger than the price. Invariants are rules every record must obey. If a save would break one, it is refused, and no one has to remember to check.
stories.concept.module: A big company app has a sales area, a warehouse area and a payroll area, each with its own words. Module says which area a concept belongs to. From another area you point to it by saying the area first, like 'sales::Customer', so two areas can both have a 'Customer'.
stories.concept.name: A card index needs a title on its box. The concept's name is that title, written without spaces, such as 'Customer'. Everything else refers to it: the table, the web address, the screens, the queries. It cannot be repeated in the same app.
stories.concept.renamedFrom: You rename 'Client' to 'Customer', but the database still holds the old table full of data. Renamed from tells NPDev 'this is the same thing under a new name', so it renames the table instead of deleting one and creating an empty one.
stories.concept.rollups: A photo has a count of likes, and nobody should add it up each time the page opens. A rollup is a stored total that NPDev keeps equal to the rows of another kind, such as the number of Like rows pointing at the photo. It is updated on every like or unlike, and no one can type it by hand.
stories.concept.satelliteOf: The identity pack knows who the users are, and your app also wants each user to have a shoe size. You cannot change the pack. A satellite is an extra card stapled to the pack's card, one for one. The pack stays untouched and your own data hangs off it.
stories.concept.softDelete: An accountant deletes a customer by mistake on Friday evening. With soft delete nothing is truly erased: the row is only marked as deleted and hidden from lists. A restore action brings it back, and its unique values can be reused meanwhile.
stories.concept.specializes: A hospital has patients, and the maternity ward also needs due dates. Specializes starts a new concept from an existing one, with all its boxes, rules and events, and lets you add more. The original is fixed at the version used, so a later change does not surprise you.
stories.concept.specializesFloat: By default, the base you copied from is frozen at the version your app was built with, and building stops if the base changes. Float says 'follow the newest version instead'. It is useful when you want the improvements the base's author ships, and you accept the surprise.
stories.concept.system: The list of passwords sits in the back office and is never meant for customers. A system concept is owned by the platform: it gets no web address, no menu, no export and no AI tool. Only the login code touches it, so a password hash can never leak through an ordinary screen.
stories.concept.temporal: A product's price changes in March and again in September, and last year's invoices must still show last year's price. A temporal concept keeps several rows for the same thing, each valid for its own dates. Asking 'as of 15 March' returns the row that applied then.
stories.concept.truthLevel: A new concept is like a draft recipe: tried once, or tested a hundred times? Truth level is a label from T0 to T6 saying how well it has been verified. A release check can refuse to ship an app whose concepts are below the level you require.
stories.concept.ui: A record can look good with no extra work, but sometimes you want a nicer title, two columns in the form or a default sort. This keyword gathers those looks for the whole concept in one place, without changing what the data means.
stories.concept.uid: People change names, and a concept's name changes with them. A uid is a fingerprint stamped on the concept once and never reused. When the name differs but the fingerprint matches, NPDev knows it is the same concept, so a rename needs no further hint.
stories.conceptAccess.public: A bakery wants its menu visible on a website without anyone logging in. The public grant opens a read-only window onto chosen rows and chosen boxes, and nothing else. Nobody outside can ever change anything through it. It is the shop window, not the shop door.
stories.conceptAccess.read: Each salesperson should see their own customers, not the whole book. The read rule is a one-line condition checked for every record: who is asking, which team, which tenant. A record for which it is false is simply invisible, as if it did not exist.
stories.conceptAccess.write: Everyone on the team may look at a task, but only its owner may change or delete it. The write rule is a one-line condition checked per record. If it is false for the person asking, the change is refused, even if they could read it.
stories.domainType.baseType: 'Postal code' is stored as text, 'Price' as a number with decimals. The base type is the plain kind of value behind a domain type. Every box that uses the domain type is stored that way.
stories.domainType.examples: Telling people a tax number looks like '123-45-678' helps more than a rule can. Examples are sample values for a domain type. They appear in help texts and are used in tests, so users and AI authors see what a good value looks like.
stories.domainType.format: A phone number looks different from a plain number: spaces, a plus sign, a country code. Format is a hint about how the value is written, for example an input pattern. It is shown to people and to AI authors so that they write it the same way.
stories.domainType.name: Instead of repeating 'text, up to 8 letters, uppercase' in thirty places, you call it 'PostalCode' once. The domain type's name is how every box that wants it asks for it by name.
stories.domainType.normalization: People type ' ANA@Mail.com ' with stray spaces and capitals, and the same address ends up twice. Normalization lists the tidying steps, such as trim and lowercase, applied before the value is checked and stored. Everyone's input ends up in one clean form.
stories.domainType.ui: Every telephone box should look the same, with the same placeholder and the same width. This keyword gives the look of a domain type once. Every box using that type inherits it, so you do not repeat it in each form.
stories.domainType.validation: A postal code has exactly five digits, a percentage is between 0 and 100. Validation gathers those limits in one place for a domain type, and every box of that type obeys them. Change the limit once and all of them follow.
stories.enumOption.badge: In a list of rides, 'Cancelled' looks calmer with a small red tag. A badge is that short coloured label next to a choice. People can scan a long list and spot the status without reading each word.
stories.enumOption.default: When someone creates a ticket, the status should already say 'Open'. Default marks the choice that is selected from the start, so people only change it when they have a reason.
stories.enumOption.deprecated: Last year's 'Pending' status is gone, but old records still carry it. Deprecated keeps the old choice readable on existing records but stops offering it for new ones. Nothing breaks, and nobody can pick it from now on.
stories.enumOption.description: 'On hold' could mean the customer is waiting or the company is. A description is one sentence saying exactly what a choice means, so everyone picks it for the same reason.
stories.enumOption.group: A long list of ticket types is easier with headings such as 'Hardware' and 'Software'. Group is the heading under which a choice sits in the dropdown. The person reads a short list per heading instead of one long list.
stories.enumOption.icon: A small truck next to 'Shipped' and a tick next to 'Delivered' make a list readable at a glance. Icon is the name of the little picture shown beside a choice, so people recognise it before reading it.
stories.enumOption.label: Behind the scenes the value is 'IN_PROGRESS', but on the screen it should say 'In progress', or 'Em andamento' for someone reading Portuguese. Label is the text shown for a choice, a plain word or one per language.
stories.enumOption.order: Statuses read best in the order of the work: Open, In progress, Done, not alphabetical. Order gives each choice its position in dropdowns and filters, lower numbers first. Choices without a number follow, in the order they were written.
stories.enumOption.value: A status needs a steady name that the database stores, even if the screen text changes next year. Value is that stored word, such as 'DONE'. Reports, filters and rules all refer to it.
